speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST DAY, QUEBEC-DISCOVERY DAY, NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the feast day of St. John the Baptist, the patron saint of French Canada. I am sure I speak for all hon. members of this house and especially, may I add, for those of the English language, when on this day I extend to our countrymen of French language and culture in the province of Quebec and elsewhere in Canada an expression of sincere good wishes and deep respect. Down the years French Canadians have drawn on deep reservoirs of courage and faith, dedication and vitality, in making their indispensable contribution to the development of our country while maintaining their special loyalty and devotion to their own rights and traditions within that country.
On this day of commemoration for one of the founding races in the great partnership of confederation I think we would do well to remember that diversity and not uniformity of race and culture is the essential and basic characteristic of Canadianism. This need not, however-I suggest must not-lead to any sacrifice of unity in the achievement of a common Canadian purpose. Other Canadians can share in the pride of French Canadians in their own traditions, their own culture and their own language, just as all Canadians of whatever origin and culture can share in the resolve to work together to realize a common future and a good future within confederation.
This is also, Mr. Speaker, what is known in Newfoundland, I believe, as Discovery day. It is a day which has particular meaning in the history of Canada, for it was on this day 466 years ago that the redoubtable explorer John Cabot had the great good fortune to discover a land that became the ancient colony and is now the Canadian province of Newfoundland.
I am certain that all hon. members of this house will join me in paying a sincere tribute to the vigorous, warm hearted and courageous people of that land. How fortunate we are to have them in confederation. We owe much to John Cabot, Mr. Speaker.

French Canadians are justified in being proud of their past and of their present contribution.
On this significant day in the history of Canada, I extend my best wishes to all French Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to join the preceding speakers in offering my congratulations to my fellow countrymen in the province of Quebec as well as in the other provinces, on our national holiday.
On this occasion I would also like to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) who, in the name of English speaking Canadians, was kind enough to offer congratulations to my fellow countrymen.
In the last few years an unusual evolution has been taking place in all spheres in the province of Quebec. It is by taking that evolution into account that the new Canadian government wants confederation to develop from now on according to the principle of equality between the two peoples who founded our nation, allowance being made for the contribution of other national groups to the cultural enrichment of our country.
Some of my fellow citizens suggest that we follow the way towards separatism. As far as I am concerned, I am convinced that this is bound to lead to serious disillusions. The only course acceptable is the one which will allow us to become equal partners in a renewed confederation.


Such is the purpose of the new Canadian government and such is the wish of the major part of our people. This wish I express with joy and pride on this national day.
I should like also to congratulate our colleagues and our countrymen from Newfoundland on this anniversary of the day of discovery.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Garland (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING SALES TAX ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated on Friday to the hon. member for Medicine Hat I should like to make an explanation today with regard to the application of the sales tax on building materials and production machinery.
In the budget speech the Minister of Finance indicated that relief would be granted where a manufacturer or contractor is prevented by a fixed price contract from including the new tax in his selling price. The provision for this relief is found in paragraph 13 of the excise tax resolution.
This provision for refunds covers all building materials and production machinery for which exemption from tax has been withdrawn by the resolution. It covers both

manufacturers and contractors but the procedure to be followed in these two cases differs.
The first situation where relief is granted is where a person, such as a manufacturer or licensed wholesaler, is required to pay-sales tax on his sales after budget date but is prevented by reason of a contract signed before June 14, 1963 from adding this tax to the price at which he sells the said goods. In order to qualify for a refund the goods must be sold and delivered before June 14, 1964. The relief will take the form of a refund of the tax to the manufacturer or licensed wholesaler, or the granting of a deduction for an amount equal to the tax from the total amount of sales tax otherwise payable by the manufacturer or wholesaler for the month. The manufacturer or wholesaler does not have to make formal application for the refund. In practice he will likely refrain from paying the tax in question to the government and will satisfy the tax auditor by producing the written contract.
The second situation where relief is granted is where a person, such as a building contractor, has not paid the tax directly. He finds on the one hand that the building materials he must purchase after budget date have been increased in price by the addition of the sales tax but on the other hand he is prevented from making a corresponding increase in the price of the building he is constructing by reason of a fixed price contract signed by him before June 14, 1963. The relief in this case takes the form of a payment by the Minister of National Revenue to the contractor equal to the amount of the tax paid on the goods purchased by the contractor. In order to qualify for this payment the goods must be delivered before June 14, 1964 and the contractor may make application to the Minister of National Revenue at any time but not later than June 14, 1966.
It will be noted that the contract fixing a price must be in writing and have been signed by the parties thereto before June 14, 1963. It should also be noted that refunds, however, cannot be made until after this house has passed the enabling legislation.
There are different types of contractual obligations, and where a person is in doubt as to whether or not his contract comes within the relieving provision it is recommended that the contractor or vendor submit a copy to the Department of National Revenue for review. We are presently reviewing various contracts which have been referred to the Department of National Revenue.
When the sales tax exemptions for building materials and production machinery and

1.	Articles and materials for the sole use of any bona fide public hospital certified to be such by the Department of National Health and Welfare continue to be exempt. This exemption includes building materials purchased to build a hospital.

3.	Municipalities will continue to benefit from the exemption from tax on their purchases of the goods listed in schedule III under the heading "Municipalities". These include:
Culverts; diesel fuel oil for use in generating electricity; equipment at a price in excess of $500 per unit specially designed for road making, road cleaning, or fire fighting; fire hoze and nozzles; fire truck chassis; laminated timber for bridges; precast concrete shapes for bridges in public highway systems; structural steel and aluminum for bridges.
The excise tax resolution proposes that goods forming part of sewerage and drainage systems be exempt from sales tax when sold to or imported by a municipality for its own use and not for resale. This exemption will also cover purchases of materials for sewerage and drainage systems by subdividers or building contractors who are required to instal these services and turn them over to a municipality.
4.	Crushed stone, sand, gravel and fieldstone continue to be exempt.
5.	Farm machinery including farm tractors and equipment used in commercial fishing continue to be exempt.
I should add that the Department of National Revenue is doing its utmost to be of assistance to all concerned. Any person manufacturing or producing goods which he has reason to believe might now be taxable should get in touch with the nearest excise tax or customs office. These officers are to supply him with a brief questionnaire the answers to which will indicate whether or not he is required to be licensed. He will be supplied with copies of the Excise Tax Act and the budget resolutions as well as a copy of the general regulations. Although the initiative rests with

As there seems to have been some misunderstanding as to the level at which the sales tax applies, I should point out that it is a manufacturers' tax and, therefore, applies at the first step in the distribution process. Perhaps I can best illustrate this by reference to its application to building materials used in the construction of a single detached house financed under the N.H.A. which act is administered by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for which I report to parliament.
The average single detached house financed under N.H.A. in 1962 had a total cost of $15,233 of which $12,204 was for construction. It is estimated that of the $12,204 for construction costs, building materials account for $5,500, the remainder being labour costs and allowances for overhead and profit, etc.
In assessing the effect of the sales tax, two circumstances must be taken into account. First, even prior to the recent budget announcement, the sales tax was being paid on certain building materials. Manufactured kitchen cabinets, electrical wiring and plumbers' piping were among these. These items accounted for about 5 per cent of the value of building materials used in the average house. Second, the sales tax is applied to the manufacturers' sale price, that is: before the mark-up for overhead and profit applied by dealers and other distributors of the building materials.
When allowance is made for these considerations, it is estimated that the 11 per cent sales tax to be applied to building materials not formerly taxed will be based on the manufacturers' sale prices of $3,913. This implies an increase in tax for the average N.H.A. house of $430.
Of course, when we look at the effect on an N.H.A. financed house we must also take into account the effects of other measures included in the budget. I refer particularly to the increased loan amount that will be available in the N.H.A. and the reduction in the maximum N.H.A. rate of interest. The effect of these measures is, in fact, to reduce the down payment and leave the monthly carrying charges approximately the same.
I hope the explanations I have given today will prove to be helpful. It is realized, of course, that in an over-all explanatory statement of this kind it is impossible to envisage and answer all individual situations and cover all possible questions. I suggest, however, that there will be other opportunities where it is customary to deal with such


particulars in greater detail. These opportunities will come when the house is in committee to debate the budget resolutions and, subsequently, to consider the provisions of the bill to amend the Excise Tax Act.
Meanwhile the department will continue to answer questions referred to it and assist the taxpayers in any of their problems.
In order to be of assistance to persons who believe they are entitled to relief because they are a party to a fixed price contract, as explained earlier, the department is willing to examine their contracts if they wish to forward them to the customs and excise division in Ottawa before they go to the work of preparing their refund claims.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Robichaud (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: NORTH PACIFIC TREATY
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON PROGRESS OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
I should like at this point to make a further report to the house on the progress of the north Pacific treaty negotiations which commenced in Washington, D.C. on June 6. These negotiations recessed on June 21 and are tc recommence this autumn.
As many hon. members already know, the present international convention for the high seas fisheries of the north Pacific ocean came into force June 12, 1953, for a definite period of ten years, after which it could be terminated on one year's notice by any one of the three parties, that is to say Canada, Japan er the United States. The ten years are now over and the recent conference was held at the request of Japan to consider the possible need for modification of the convention.
The present convention, alone among all fisheries treaties, embodies the principle of ahstention. Under this principle if one or more of the parties are exploiting a fish stock to the full and are restricting their fishing by regulations based on scientific research in order to maintain that fish stock at a productive level, the other party or parties will abstain from entering the fishery.
In accordance with this principle Japan, under the present convention, is required to abstain from fishing the important salmon, halibut and herring stocks of North American origin, and Canada abstains from fishing salmon in the Bering sea. Our fisheries have in this way had a very large measure of protection from the expanding Japanese high seas fishing operations. There have been some difficulties in the application of the principle of abstention, but our experts believe that no stocks which do not qualify now remain under abstention and that all stocks which qualify are presently under abstention. Continuation of the present convention, including
1474	HOUSE OF
North Pacific Fisheries Treaty the abstention principle, is thus very important to the Pacific fisheries of Canada.
This convention has not been popular in Japan because it has restricted the expansion of their fisheries in the northeastern Pacific. Early during the present negotiations the Japanese delegation proposed a revision of the treaty to eliminate the principle of abstention, which they claim to be monopolistic and contrary to generally accepted principles of freedom of fishing on the high seas. With this principle removed the convention would provide for joint conservation measures, but would not afford protection to the fisheries which have been brought by Canada and the United States to high levels of utilization and productivity through great efforts on the part of our two countries.
During the negotiations the Canadian delegation supported the principle of abstention, claiming that the last ten years have shown it to be an equitable and workable means of maintaining the unique fisheries to which it applies in the north Pacific. Our delegation pointed out that the abstention principle had majority support at the conference on the law of the sea and has achieved a large measure of international recognition. The Canadian delegation also pointed out that not only are the stocks of salmon, halibut and herring, to which the abstention principle applies, fully utilized by our fishermen but have been maintained at their present high productive levels by strict regulation of our fisheries based on scientific research.
Furthermore, our countries have brought these fisheries to their present high levels of utilization and productivity at considerable cost, not only for research and enforcement of restrictions on our fishermen but, especially in the case of salmon, through positive fish culture measures and through abstaining ourselves from using the rivers in which the salmon are bred for other purposes such as power development, irrigation, waste disposal, etc. The maintenance of these fisheries, already difficult and expensive, would become almost impossible if the benefits of these measures were not reserved for our own fishermen. The Canadian and United States delegations were in complete accord in insisting on the continued inclusion of the abstention principle in the north Pacific treaty.
During the conference there has been an exchange of views which has clarified the positions of the three parties. The convention has defined the problems and indicated in a preliminary way some of the possible means of solving them. One of the most difficult problems is caused by the intermingling on the fishing grounds of halibut which require


protection under the abstention principle with larger stocks of other bottom fish which are not now intensively fished by the United States and Canada and from which Japan has no obligation to abstain. The problem here is to devise means by which Japan can make use of these stocks, some of which are already being fished extensively by the Soviet union, while at the same time affording protection to the halibut fisheries which have been maintained at a high level by a convention between the United States and Canada which is one of the oldest and most successful fisheries treaties in existence.
Although Canada, Japan and the United States all agree that a convention among our three countries is necessary to maintain the fisheries of the north Pacific in the interests of the fishing industries of our three countries, no agreement has yet been reached regarding modification of the present convention to this end. The Canadian delegation believes that all these problems, including both the special protection for our unique salmon, halibut and herring fisheries and the conservation of the north Pacific fisheries generally, can be solved within the framework of the present convention and will endeavour in the further discussions planned later this year to bring this about.
I would reiterate, Mr. Speaker, that any tentative agreements reached during these negotiations will be fully discussed before the standing committee on marine and fisheries before final acceptance by the government.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the official opposition I welcome this statement from the minister, but I think in common with Canadians everywhere I regret the unfortunate circumstances which made an agreement of this type apparently not possible at this convention in Washington.
However, I do agree with the minister that the retention of the abstention principle with regard to this fisheries treaty is of vital importance to Canada. be maintained under all circumstances for the future orderly development of the living resources of the north Pacific.

speechtext: What steps have been taken and what recommendations have been advanced by the government of Canada since 1956 to give to NATO, apart from the military, a political and an economic content?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RECOMMENDATIONS RESPECTING POLITICAL AND ECONOMIC CONTENT
speechtext:
Information about individual recommendations and activities of NATO member states in the NATO council is classified. In December 1956 NATO published the report of the committee of three on non-military co-operation which established guide lines to improve and extend political and economic consultation. The present Prime Minister of Canada was a member of the committee of three. As a result of this report, which still forms the basis for the non-military activities of the alliance, NATO established the political advisers committee, the committee of economic advisers, the science committee and a program of visiting NATO fellowships. Canada supported the establishment of these bodies and actively participates in their deliberations.
There have also been established the organization for economic development and co-operation and the development assistance committee whose membership consist not only of members of NATO but other countries as well. The functions of these bodies are complementary to the purposes outlined in article 2 of the NATO treaty.
Since 1956 there have been impressive strides within the alliance in the scope and content of consultation on non-military problems. At the recent NATO meeting in Ottawa the Canadian delegation expressed the determination of the Canadian government to play a full and constructive role in this aspect of the day to day work of the NATO council.
IMr. Drury.]

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SITUATION
speechtext:
I thank the hon. gentleman, first of all, for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question, and for his congratulations. I should tell him however that it is not permissible in this house to mention any hon. member's age, after the age of 30.
In answer to the hon. gentleman's question, may I say that the basic difficulty in Laos-is that although a provisional government representing the three important political tendencies was established last summer when the international agreement on Laos was signed in Geneva, the administration and armed forces of Laos have not yet been integrated. The country therefore remains in effect divided into zones controlled by the forces of the right wing, the neutralist party and the Pathet Lao.
During the past few months there has been a marked deterioration, I regret to say, in the political and military situation in that particular country. The Pathet Lao with the help of some dissident neutralists, has forced the main neutralist army to give up several important points in the plain of Jars. Within

the past ten days there have been reports of fighting also in the region of Attopeu, in the southern part of the country.
The government has been following these developments with concern because of our membership with India and Poland on the international commission for supervision and control in Laos. The commission has been doing its best, in very difficult circumstances, to exercise a calming and stabilizing influence, and to report on the situation objectively to the governments signatory to the Geneva agreement. It has been our view that the commission should send or station its representatives in troubled areas. A commission team has in fact been stationed on the plain of Jars at the request of the prime minister of Laos, since April 29. The Polish delegation is unfortunately not represented on this team.
Last week the Indian and Canadian commissioners decided to send their military advisers to the Attopeu area to report to them on the situation there. The Polish commissioner did not send his military adviser. The Pathet Lao radio has commented adversely on the visit of the Canadian and Indian military advisers to Attopeu, and it is this comment which has probably given rise to the news reports referred to by the hon. member.
The commissioners are now deciding, in the light of their military advisers' reports, what they can usefully do to help restore peace to the Attopeu area. I can only say that Canada, as a member of that commission, is doing everything it can in that very disturbed area.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, June 21, consideration of the motion of Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Nowlan.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I began my remarks on Friday I was outlining what the budget proposals set out to do. I pointed out that major changes were required in the structure of Canadian industry if more jobs were to be provided in the future, and I suggested that our chronic payments deficits were the root cause of the difficulties that confront us. Wrapped up in this is the extent of absentee control of the Canadian economy. We must take steps to check this steadily mounting absentee control if we are to resolve our difficulties and remain masters of our destiny. It was for this reason I outlined the views of the government respecting the best way of preserving harmonious relations with foreign investors in Canadian industry. I believe this is the first time this has been done in any formal way.
The budget proposals include a variety of measures designed to plug loopholes in the tax system, and two major measures for producing additional revenue this year and to a greater extent next year. The latter include the requirement that corporations should file their tax returns and pay their taxes on the same dates as individuals do, and the withdrawal of the sales tax exemption on building materials and production machinery.
In the opinion of the government it would have been unwise not to take some preliminary steps to reduce the budgetary deficit. Various methods of doing this were considered but they boiled down essentially to three. These were, first, a substantial increase in the sales tax across the board. This would have meant an increase in the ordinary living costs of everyone in Canada regardless of income, and was resisted for this reason. The second method was an increase in personal income taxes. If this were to produce the desired amount of revenue it would have been necessary to apply the increase at all levels. Again, the government was reluctant
[Mr. Olson.1

to add to the burdens of those in the lower income brackets who have already had to bear the burden of considerably increased living costs. To have been effective in producing a substantial increase in revenue, an increase in personal income tax would have had to be accompanied by an equally substantial increase in corporation income taxes. This would have slowed production and reduced employment.
The third possibility was the removal of the exemption from sales tax on building materials and production machinery. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, no government could be happy about doing any of these things. All of them would be bound to be unpopular. None of them is pleasant. Nevertheless, given the premise that some kind of a start should be made to bring our affairs into balance and to reduce the deficit, it was decided that the withdrawal of the exemption was much the least objectionable of the three courses mentioned.
We all know that any tax increase adds to costs and has some ill effects on production. More income tax or a higher sales tax on the things that everybody buys would have had a far worse effect-a worse effect, especially, on employment. I hope that there will be a lot more discussion about the objectives of the budget and about the specific proposals put forward during the remainder of this debate. I shall have something more to say about this a little later.
However, as much more attention has been given so far to the assistance received in preparing the budget than to the budget itself I should first like to say something on this latter subject. When I was appointed Minister of Finance I believed it was my urgent duty to provide a national accounting as soon as possible. There was a vital need to develop new policies for the encouragement of employment, and that meant preparing in my department major legislation for the municipal development and loan board and the Canada development corporation. That was in addition to all the work which had been accumulating during the election.
Faced with tasks of this magnitude and urgency, the Department of Finance was seriously overburdened. There is a limit to what it is fair and possible to ask even of men of such devotion to duty and such ability as the officials of the department. I therefore decided that it would be desirable to bring in some temporary help to assist with the drafting of legislation and the preparation of the budget. My colleagues agreed with me and I secured the services of the four men whose names have been mentioned in the debate. As soon as they arrived in Ottawa I gave instructions that they should take or be

given the oath of secrecy and this was done. Everyone who worked on the budget swore an oath of secrecy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
From then on, Mr. Speaker, I considered everyone concerned, whether they were full time members of the civil service or consultants attached to the Department of Finance, to be in the same position as confidential officials.
Special mention has been made of the fact that Messrs. Stanley and O'Connell did not receive remuneration from the government for their services other than a per diem allowance to cover their expenses. It has been suggested that if they had been paid a salary this would have avoided a question of conflict of interest; to put it another way, that things would have "looked better" if this procedure had been followed.
In retrospect I obviously agree it would have looked better to arrange things in this way. But in practice, however, if it is accepted that the men in question were planning to return to their firms within a relatively short time, it is questionable whether the actual payment of salaries would have changed the situation in any real or material way.
There have been many discussions about the question of conflict of interest. In the last analysis these matters must be resolved by a man's conscience, integrity and his sense of personal honesty. Members of parliament and members of the civil service are in positions of trust and no one would suggest that any of them would use information for personal gain which came to them because of their positions. Surely the same criteria must apply to all others engaged in government service, either on a permanent or a temporary basis. I have complete confidence in the integrity of the many senior civil servants and of the special consultants who assisted me in the preparation of the budget. As I said on Friday, June 14, I take personal responsibility not only for the budget itself but I accept personal responsibility for the secrecy with which it was prepared.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have no complaint about the questions that have been raised by hon. members on this matter, in so far as they have been directed to myself. I could have taken the safe, cautious and traditional course of producing a budget at some later date. I decided, and it was my decision, to take steps to speed up the proceedings so that
The Budget-Mr. Gordon Canadians might know where they stood, and might be informed about the policies the government proposed as quickly as possible. What I am particularly sorry about, however, is that my decision has caused a debate which has reflected on the integrity of able and patriotic men who were willing to come here and serve their country to the best of their ability. I can only hope that what has been said and insinuated about these three men in the past ten days will not discourage other able and honourable Canadians from serving this government and other governments in the future.
Let me now return to the budget itself, which is the subject of this debate. It is complex, and it is novel in many of the proposals it contains. I became convinced that one of them, the proposed 30 per cent tax on foreign takeovers of Canadian firms, while highly desirable in its objective, would not work in practice in the form in which it was presented. Having reached this conclusion, I recommended to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that it should be withdrawn immediately pending a further examination. I have now made that examination and have come to the conclusion that this tax is not practicable for this budget.
It was not easy last Wednesday to decide to withdraw the tax. However I thought, and the government thought, this was the proper thing to do and that the withdrawal should be announced to the house at the earliest possible moment. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, and in the light of the stock market action at the time, it was best to have made the announcement when I did. I have been criticized for informing the three special consultants of my decision to withdraw the tax on takeovers before the announcement was made publicly. All I can say in reply to this is that, in view of their work on the budget and the fact they were sworn to secrecy, I believed it proper to inform them of the change I proposed to make, just as I thought it proper to inform the two senior permanent officials of the department concerned. If the consultants were to have been treated differently while they were attached to the department, then they never should have been taken on in the first place.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it has been suggested that the house was misled as to the circumstances surrounding the withdrawal of the takeover tax. I certainly had no intention of misleading anyone. If some hon. members feel that they were misled, I apologize to them. But nevertheless, having reread Hansard carefully, I am convinced in my own mind that my answers were at all times accurate and proper replies to the questions asked. On

The Budget

Mr. Gordon Wednesday last, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) inquired as to whether I had advised Mr. Kierans or anyone else as to withdrawal of the takeover tax. The suggestion, as I understood the question at the time, was anyone else connected with the stock market. In my reply I said I had given no information to Mr. Kierans or anybody else. I added that I had, of course, talked to the Prime Minister and members of the cabinet. I said in my answer, if I remember correctly, certain members of the cabinet, because all of them were not present at the time.
On Thursday, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) asked whether I had consulted, he used the word "consulted", my three outside advisers before withdrawing the tax. I replied to him that no one but the Prime Minister and members of the cabinet were consulted. This was absolutely true. Perhaps I should have added that I had informed the departmental officials, including the three consultants, of the decision. But I would remind hon. members that this was not the question asked. On Friday, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked whether anyone else besides the top officials of the Department of Finance had been informed of the decision. My answer was, yes, I had informed the deputy minister, the assistant deputy minister dealing with taxation, and Messrs. Stanley, Conway and O'Connell.
It has been suggested that this answer on Friday differed from the answer I had given to the Leader of the Opposition on Wednesday. The answers differ because the questions were not the same. The question asked me on Wednesday was whether I had advised Mr. Kierans of the Montreal stock exchange on the previous evening or advised anyone else that day. I took it for granted that the question referred to other stock exchange officials who had come to see me, and I think everybody knew they had come to see me. It did not occur to me that the Leader of the Opposition meant to include in his question members of my departmental staff, and frankly I do not believe the Leader of the Opposition intended at the time to do so. If he had so intended, he would have framed his question differently. And if he had framed it differently, I would have answered it as forthrightly as I answered the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on Friday.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If there has been a misunderstanding in this matter, I can only apologize to the house, but I repeat there was no intention on my part to mislead anyone.


In the course of the debate a number of proposals have been made by hon. members respecting other items in the budget. For example, the hon. member for Digby-Anna-polis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) questioned the desirability of giving the Minister of National Revenue discretion to deal with questions involving dividend stripping. I can assure him I shall give this careful consideration before the bill comes before the house.
I think it was the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) who raised a question about the desirability of making certain amendments with respect to pipe line companies retroactive to April 10, 1962. This was done to avoid some very complicated drafting, and because I was informed that the companies in question would not benefit from such retroactivity in any way. However, I shall look into the matter again and consider it before the bill is introduced.
I hope very much, Mr. Speaker, that other hon. members will bring forward their proposals for improvements. It seems to me that is what a budget debate is for, and I can assure the house that all such proposals will be considered very carefully. If they are practical proposals that will improve the legislation, appropriate changes will be made either when the budget resolutions or the bills are presented for approval.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is one thing I should like to say in conclusion. In the past week some hon. members of the house-I hope not too many-and some people outside the house have made it plain that they would like to see me leave public life.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXEMPTING REVENUES FROM CONTRIBUTIONS TO PENSION FUND

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Lessard (Lake St. John) moved:
subtopic: AMENDMENT EXEMPTING REVENUES FROM CONTRIBUTIONS TO PENSION FUND
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should study the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act so that all revenue deriving from a contribution to a recognized pension fund be exempt from income tax up to a maximum of $3,000 a year.
He said:
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, this notice of motion I have introduced and which is being considered today follows many other resolutions designed to improve the financial situation of those who have reached retirement age. Most of those workers have contributed to pension funds by way of deduction from their salaries in order to get some security and an income when the time comes for them to retire, at 65 years of age.
The motion provides:
That all revenue deriving from a contribution to a recognized pension fund be exempt from income tax up to a maximum of $3,000 a year.
Mr. Speaker, when a worker has contributed all his life to the welfare of the country, he is entitled to our gratefulness. At present, those who are nearing retirement age dread the day when they will have to live even more sparingly than before.
Income Tax Exemptions
Having worked throughout their life, without even having had the opportunity to visit their country, to the development of which they have contributed, they see themselves, at 65 years of age, cast aside, condemned to be ignored till their death by the other members of the community.
Statistics show that a large number of pensioners die during the first years following their retirement on account of the sudden change and of worries about their lower income, since in several cases, they still have heavy family responsibilities.
I know that when we are contributing to a pension fund, contributions are not taxable. But, as these amounts are invested in state funds and in private trust funds, I believe that they are highly profitable to the government through the years, since these funds are used to finance the government or companies whose profits are then taxed by the government.
Therefore, I feel the government should accept that recommendation and take it into consideration when implementing the portable pension program it has just put on the order paper.
I know there is much to be said on the subject, and we shall no doubt have the opportunity to do so later.
I do not wish to spend too much time on the matter, because I know how interesting it will be to hear what other members will have to say in that regard.
So I shall end my remarks here and yield to those who want to take part in this debate. I ask them to judge that motion on its merits so that they may give credit to those who helped build this country in which we live and develop this strong nation of which we are proud.
(Text):

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. Benson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT EXEMPTING REVENUES FROM CONTRIBUTIONS TO PENSION FUND
speechtext:
The question
which the hon. member has raised is an interesting one. I must admit that when I first read his motion I did not fully understand its meaning. It reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should study the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act so that all revenue deriving from a contribution to a recognized pension fund be exempt from income tax up to a maximum of $3,000 a year.
When I first read these words I thought the hon. member wished to have pension plan deductions increased from the $1,500 which is allowed at present to $3,000. It occurred to me, though, that perhaps he wanted the income received by a pension fund, from the investment of funds contributed by employers and

Income Tax Exemptions employees and put into investments in bonds and securities, to be exempt in the hands of the fund, which is already the case. After listening to the hon. member I understand that what he is really seeking is to have the exemptions of people over 65 years of age increased from the present limit of $1,000, or $2,500 in the case of a married couple, to $3,000 per person or perhaps to $3,000 in total if they have money coming to them from a pension fund. Which of these he desires is not clear in the resolution.
I think that under our present legislation a situation arises where people in the lower income group are treated differently from people with higher incomes who have reached the age of 65 and who have income from various sources whether from pension funds or otherwise. At present, a person who is relatively wealthy when he reaches the age of 65, and whose wife is also receiving income, may claim an exemption of $1,000, as may his wife, plus $500, plus medical and donations exemption of at least $100. This means the two persons, each of whom has an income in excess of $1,000, may be eligible for total exemptions in the amount of $3,200. On the other hand, in cases when a married man is in a lower income tax group-let us assume his wife does not receive income in excess of $1,000-may claim only a total exemption of $2,600, that is, the exemption of $1,000 for himself, $1,000 for his wife and $500 because he is beyond the age of 65, plus $100 basic exemption for medical and charitable payments.
I agree with the hon. member who introduced this motion that this situation is unfair to persons who are in a lower income tax bracket. However, I believe the motion is unnecessary. I know this matter has been raised with the Minister of Finance and I am sure it will be considered carefully in the future so that the anomaly now existing in the Income Tax Act may perhaps be corrected in the future.
At this time I should like to review some of the provisions of the Income Tax Act with respect to pensions-provisions which I think are fair and reasonable both to those who are contributing to pensions and to those who are receiving funds by way of pension. First of all, however, with regard to exemptions generally, let me repeat that I agree there is an argument in favour of increasing to $3,000 the total exemptions for a man and his wife, when they reach the age of 65. However, I do not think this should be confined to amounts received from a pension fund. I do not agree that pension receipts should be treated differently from funds derived from any other source when a man and his wife reach the age of 65. In con-

nection with this conclusion, I should like to refer to the Income Tax Act and some of its provisions with regard to pension funds. Looking at section 11 (1) (i), we find that amounts contributed by the taxpayer to or under registered pension fund or plan are deductible from income in an amount not exceeding in the aggregate $1,500 in the year if retained by his employer from his remuneration in respect of services rendered in the year; or paid into or under the fund or plan by the taxpayer as part of his dues for the year as a member of a trade union. That is, the individual has the right to deduct from his income his actual contributions to the pension fund up to $1,500 a year. In addition, he may deduct an additional $1,500 in respect of payments making up for past contributions should he have entered the pension plan late in life. Similarly, under section 11 (1)	(g) and section 11 (1)	(h) of the
Income Tax Act an employer has the right to deduct from his income contributions which he may make on behalf of an employee to a registered pension plan in order to build up a pension fund for the benefit of the employee when he retires. The amounts he may deduct in these circumstances are similar to those of the employee, that is, he may deduct an amount up to $1,500 in respect of each employee he has for present services and he may deduct an additional amount in respect of past services. In addition, under section 76 of the Act, an employer may make deductions with regard to a lump sum payment to build up the actuarial amount necessary to provide pensions for employees on retirement. Section 5 (1) (a) of the act excludes amounts which are contributed by an employer to build up a pension fund for an employee from income of the employee during a specific year. Thus under the present provisions of our Income Tax Act an employer and employee may together make current contributions of up to $3,000 to a registered pension fund all of which are deductible from the taxable income of the employer or employee. In addition amounts may be deducted in respect of past services.
When I first looked at this resolution put forward by the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) I felt he was seeking to have this amount increased beyond the present $1,500 level for each during a year up to an amount of $3,000 each, and I took the trouble to look into what it would cost the treasury. Such an increase would cost in the area of six or seven million dollars annually. Throughout a man's lifetime and during the period he is employed he may make contributions to a pension fund, and deduct them

in addition to his ordinary personal exemptions, in determining the amount on which he pays tax. A person who pays into a pension fund is thus in the position where he has had an advantage over the individual working for himself who may not have been fortunate enough to contribute to a pension fund.
This was the situation up until 1957, when the idea of a registered retirement savings plan in Canada was put forward. Beginning with the 1957 taxation year individual taxpayers could obtain a limited deduction of premiums paid under registered retirement savings plans, also referred to as pensions for the self-employed, in computing their income tax each taxation year. However, as is presently the case with funds received from a pension fund, all amounts contributed by an individual to a registered retirement savings plan are taxable along with interest earned when received back by the individual. It really gives the individual the right, in effect, to somewhat average his income over his lifetime. He can by contributing to funds such as this, reduce his taxable income during years of high earnings, and then when he has reached retirement age at 65 or perhaps 60, or whenever he chooses to retire he may take these funds into his income and the amounts he receives will be taxed at lower rates at a time when he is in a much lower income tax bracket. The idea of a retirement savings plan was a fine one when introduced in 1957. It provided a chance for the individual not employed or not a member of a trade union, where people did have an opportunity to contribute towards pension funds, to set up his own pension plan and create a retirement allowance for himself when he reached 65 years of age.
The registered retirement savings fund follows the principle that an individual may contribute to a plan which is set up by him and cared for by a trustee. He may deduct an amount equivalent to 10 per cent of his income for the year, not exceeding $2,500. It would seem at first glance that he has been treated rather favourably as compared to the employee who is able only to deduct an amount up to $1,500, so provisions were put into the plan which was incorporated in the Income Tax Act whereby a person who is contributing to an ordinary pension plan would be allowed to make additional contributions to a registered retirement savings plan which he could set up on his own up to an amount of $1,000, so that he could make a total contribution of $2,500 into some sort of retirement plan, which contributions would be deductible for income tax purposes. Thus we are in a position where an individual
Income Tax Exemptions working in a plant or for an employer who has a pension plan might actually have an amount up to $4,000 each year going into retirement plans set up on his behalf, which contributions either he or his employer could deduct from income in that particular year. These funds are allowed to accumulate at interest or be invested and earn dividends, which is the case with many retirement savings plans. Many plans such as this have been set up by trust companies, banks and insurance companies. Indeed, there is a great variety of plans. There are plans which allow an individual to invest in equity stock, so that in that way he wrill not suffer from the diminishing value of the dollar. His stocks will appreciate in value as the dollar feels the effect of inflation, which is all to his benefit.
On these grounds I think there is no serious argument that funds received out of a pension plant at age 65 or at an earlier age should be treated any differently from funds from any other source. As I said previously I think there is validity in the argument that a person at age 65 who is married and receiving funds, whether they be out of a pension or otherwise, should be allowed a total deduction of $3,000; that is, both he and his wife should be allowed the extra $500 deduction permitted at age 65. As I have discovered from the hon. member's interpretation of his motion, I do not think there is any argument that funds received out of a pension plan by people who have retired should be treated any differently from income received from any other source, in that the individual has been able to deduct the amount contributed to this pension fund in arriving at his taxable income over the years.
Many people in years gone by used to buy themselves a government of Canada annuity out of their own capital funds. There is a provision in the present Income Tax Act whereby the only amount taxable in the hands of such people is the amount of the income increment to the fund over the period of investment. If one invests one's own capital in an annuity and does not deduct it at the time it is invested, then it is not taxable when it comes back. The only amount taxable in the hands of the individual under the Income Tax Act when such amount is returned to them is the sum deducted during the years of employment from their taxable income, plus interest, earned by the fund.
There has been a great deal of discussion about the portability of pensions and the right of people to move their pensions from place to place. There is on the order paper at the present time a resolution proposed by the present government providing for the full portability of pensions, and also for a

I think the idea of this pension plan as proposed in the resolution which will ultimately be discussed in the form of a bill later on will warrant support by everyone in this house. I believe this pension fund will provide a basic pension for all. It will provide the working man with the right to move his pension from place to place and will, I think, give to the people of Canada a type of social security they have never enjoyed up to this time.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would simply like to say, with respect to the hon. member's motion, now that I understand it-I must admit that I had some difficulty when I first read it-I am sympathetic to his view, if his view is that a married couple of 65 years of age should be entitled to a total exemption of $3,000 regardless of the amount of their income; that is, that there should be no difference between the rich and the poor when they reach 65 years of age. However, I cannot accept, and I do not think many hon. members can after the explanation I have given as to how pension contributions are treated throughout a person's lifetime, that pension fund receipts after age 65, which have been deductible from a person's income during his period of high earnings, should be treated any differently than any other type of income which is received by a person after he has retired.

Mr. Speaker, with the usual brevity displayed by the members of my party I would like to express our support of this resolution, for a very good reason. I think this is one field regarding which the attention of governments both present and past has been very sadly lacking.
I refer to just what is a proper amount of income to be exempted from income tax. It seems to me that the amount proposed in this


resolution of $3,000 a year is a very reasonable minimum in this day and age. After all, what is income tax; on what basis should it be applied? I am one of those who thinks that income tax is a tax that should apply only on a surplus of income, and by surplus of income I mean something over and above the bare necessities of life. Certainly in the present day and age, with the cost of living rising to its present height, this whole field needs a great deal of reconsideration. I am one of those who, with many, many people in Canada, was quite disappointed with the present government. While they seemed, like governments in the past, to realize this necessity while sitting on the opposition benches, they promptly forgot it when they again moved over to the treasury benches.
It would seem to me that every argument that could be put forward in support of this resolution as it applies to pensioners would apply equally well, and possibly even more so, to wage earners. There are certain expenses that are even greater than those incurred during the years of retirement and receipt of pension. I am thinking of such expenses as acquiring a home and raising a family. These are expenses that are not normally encountered by people who are in receipt of a pension.
While I express support for the resolution and would like to congratulate the hon. member for raising the matter for discussion at this time and for reminding the government that certainly in this field they have been rather neglectful in not recognizing this situation and doing something about it, I would say that the minimum amount expressed in the resolution should apply all across the board and should not be confined to people who are in receipt of pensions. This is something, as I have said, that has been sadly neglected in the past. I think it is about time we took a realistic look at this question and brought the exemptions from income tax up to date so they will have a more realistic meaning in the present day and age.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Benson), I had some difficulty in understanding this resolution. After the explanation of the mover of the motion, the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard), I think it is now clear what is intended. All of us must agree with the general intention of the resolution, to provide some relief in later years and try to make them as comfortable as possible. I think, however, as a member of this house that the motion in its present form would not be the most equitable means of achieving this purpose. The hon. member for Kingston outlined the history

of tax legislation concerning pensions in this country. He pointed out the general evolution of the principle of pensions. First, there were a number of persons who purchased pensions with money which they retained after taxes; then they had the privilege in later years of drawing payments from the pension plan and paying income tax only on the interest portion of the moneys invested. Then came exemptions built into the legislation to protect the person on payroll, first with respect to the contributions by the wage earner himself, then the contributions in respect of past service, and the contributions by the employer matching, in many cases, those of the employee. I think the hon. member for Kingston pointed out the total amount of exemption which could be claimed by those on payroll. Then there were provisions to deal with independently employed persons.
I disagree with the hon. member for Kingston in one respect. He said he saw no reason why income from a recognized pension fund should be treated any differently than income from other sources. I think there is a good reason why it should, and I would like, if I may, to develop two examples. We will first take employee A, who lives in Ottawa, of course-probably in the Carleton riding- who undertakes a program of systematic saving through his life and participates in a form of investment which is quite usual in this area, he buys a property, in which he lives, and has some income. It may be a duplex or a triplex, but it is a fairly modest property. He purchases that property out of income left after taxes. He enjoys no income tax exemption in respect of that type of purchase. Then in later years part of his retirement income consists of the rents from such property. He pays tax on the income before he makes the investment; then he pays income tax on the money he earns from that investment.
Contrast employee B, who is entirely on payroll. He gets an income tax exemption for his contributions to the pension plan, and the motion as presented to us would grant him an exemption on the money he derives from a pension plan, on which he had an exemption in the first place. This is a discrimination. It compounds the discrimination in respect of income from different sources. To be perfectly equitable you would have to say, in my opinion, that the exemption would be given to income from a source other than a recognized retirement savings plan or pension plan for which an income tax exemption has been given in the first place. Only on this basis would the two be treated equally.
But I think we would all agree that there is a limit to how far we can go in this kind
Income Tax Exemptions of approach. The proper approach to deal with the matter is to deal with it in terms of the exemptions which are enjoyed by older persons at the time of retirement when they need the benefit most. The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Benson) referred to the basic exemption of $1,000, the additional age exemption of $500 and the medical-charitable exemption of $100, or a total of $1,600 per person or $3,200 per couple, now enjoyed by persons regardless of the source of their income.
I submit that this is the proper approach to deal with this problem. It is a problem of exemptions under the general income tax laws, treating income from various sources equally and not discriminating in favour of income from a registered pension plan or retirement savings plan as against income from another form of life savings.
I think there is another reason why we should think twice about acting on the motion in its present form at this time. We have already had the attention of the house called, of course, to the resolution respecting the Canada pension plan found in order No. 15 on today's order paper. This was referred to by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). I think I have got the three names of his constituency correctly. This resolution refers to the Canada pension plan which it is the intention of the government to establish and for which purpose legislation will be brought before the house as soon as the resolution is adopted. Certainly we will have to look at the provisions of this legislation bearing in mind the problem which the mover of the resolution now before us has brought to our attention.
At this point I should like to digress a little and call attention to the resolution found in order No. 13 which has to do with the establishment of the Canada development corporation and which reads in part as follows:
-and generally to further the development of the resources and industries of Canada; and for such purposes to establish an investment company, to be called the Canada development corporation, with a share capital structure whereby the largest possible numbers of Canadians may directly and indirectly invest capital in and profit from the ownership of Canadian industries and undertakings and the development of Canada; to authorize a guarantee by Canada of certain obligations of the corporation-
And so on. I would hope that as a result of this proposal, which I am confident will be adopted by the house, it will be possible to recognize contributions made to the Canada development corporation for pension purposes, and I have no doubt in my mind that one of the purposes which the mover

Income Tax Exemptions of the resolution now before us has in mind might well be achieved if the government were to give consideration to the recognition of contributions to the Canada development corporation, which in my opinion represents a very convenient and desirable form of channelling the savings of Canadians.
We need savings. Canada never had a greater need for capital to further her growth than at the present time. We need measures that are designed to encourage savings in an orderly form and to channel them into the direction of Canadian resources which will be retained under Canadian ownership and whereby the equity represented in such resources will be available to finance the retirement of older citizens. I would think that such would be a highly desirable, if secondary, purpose of such legislation and I hope that when it is brought before the house there will be an opportunity for further examination.
In brief, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the resolution now before us discriminates in favour of one type of income and against another type of income, that it does not recognize the problem represented by the fact that savings are desirable from a public point of view and take many different forms and that we should not just recognize one of them. I believe that the general purpose of the resolution is laudable and all of us can support it without qualification, but such a purpose can be best achieved through an amendment to the Income Tax Act in respect of the basic exemptions enjoyed by persons who are retired.
Finally, I think that the resolution should be considered in relation to at least two proposed pieces of legislation which will come before the house whereby it is possible to consider all of the ramifications and to make the necessary adjustments at that time if such are called for.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other members of this side of the house I had some difficulty originally in deciphering the intent of the hon. member's notice of motion. At first I was under the misapprehension that my hon. friend was concerned with the deduction of $3,000 per year. At present, as the house knows, professional men and ^others in specified categories can deduct up to 10 per cent of their income to a maximum of $2,500 per year but beyond that they cannot make deductions. I was afraid that my hon. friend, who is a member of the Social Credit party, was concerned with persons making more than $25,000 per year and I was rather shocked to think that this might be his concern, inasmuch as I know that his party purports to speak for and 

represent average citizens and ordinary people. It is well known by the people of Canada, as they have shown at the polls on many occasions, that those on this side of the house are the champions of the ordinary people of this country with average incomes. Therefore I was quite concerned when I thought that the Social Credit party was now representing people who make $25,000 or over a year.
However, in listening to the hon. member I was glad to see that this was not his main concern, but rather the return of the payments and not the deduction of premiums. From the standpoint of deductions from income of persons over the age of 65 years I think that none of us would disagree with the fact that a $3,000 exemption is certainly little enough for someone who has lived in this country all his life, contributed to the country and paid his taxes. Certainly a married couple should be entitled to a $3,000 exemption.
As the first speaker on this side of the house pointed out, I think this is now the case in respect of a married couple over 65 years in that each of them can claim $1,500. The motion limits the deduction to recognized pension funds. I take it that the hon. member means registered pension funds, which is the term used in the Income Tax Act. I would deduce from his presentation of the motion that he does not wish the deduction to apply in respect of all pension plans but merely those recognized under the Income Tax Act and referred to as registered plans.
In my view there is inherent in the motion a very broad concept that is no doubt giving trouble to all of us and particularly to members of the cabinet who are concerned with the over-all financial and fiscal picture of the country at this time. There was a day not too long ago, Mr. Speaker, in the days of the laissez-faire free enterprise economy which are not too far behind us, when it was thought that a citizen should provide in large measure for his own future and well-being and that of his dependants. At one time this was possible for people who were industrious, thrifty, farsighted and able to find work.
We have, certainly since the war, come into a new concept of the responsibility of the citizen. We have, to a very large measure, made it impossible for the average citizen to look after his own future and that of his dependants in his old age. I suggest, whether we like it or no, whether we are free enterprisers or whether we are Galbraithian Liberals on this side of the house, every state has to decide where the funds are coming from, how they will be collected, and how the total wealth of the country shall be spent.

A state must also take some responsibility, if she is going to be the great collector of revenues, for the well being of her citizens in those years when they are no longer the producers in the country.
I am quoting off the cuff now, but I believe I have seen statistics to indicate that if we take corporate taxes, federal income taxes, provincial income taxes, indirect taxes and municipal taxes, for governments big and small and state with a small "s" and a big "s", there is some 55 per cent of the total production of this country in each year appropriated for the purposes of the state. Now, the minute we realize that this is what is happening, then of course, we must realize that there are two problems presented. Perhaps my figures are a little high because they include corporate taxes. However, if as I say, 50 per cent of the total production is taken for taxes, then we reach two problems.
In the first place, how is the average citizen going to provide for such necessities as his old age and the education of his children? These things are impossible for him to provide as long as the state is going to take such a great percentage of the total production as she definitely has, and as we demand. We who sit in this house know how very great are the demands of citizens for services from the state. We get nothing for nothing in this world. If the state is going to provide these services, then it is going to require these funds. It is going to have to assume responsibility for the well being of our citizens in their old age to a far greater degree than has been the case in the past.
I point out, Mr. Speaker, that there is one other problem created by this large proportion of our total national production being taken by the state. Not only are our citizens unable to provide for their own old age, but they have too little to put back into economic development of this country. This is the tragedy that we are facing now as was seen by the recent ill-destined 30 per cent takeover tax. I think all of us in this country are concerned, irrespective of the side of the house on which we may sit, irrespective of the method whereby we on this side of the house tried to prevent this taking over of our industry by foreign capital. We would like the Canadian economy, and in particular the control of our natural resources to be in the hands of the Canadian people rather than in the hands of foreign investors.
I believe that our friends south of the border have done a far better job than we have of creating people's capitalism. South of the border we see a far greater proportion of equity financing of large corporations owned by the average citizen, the working man and woman. Members of labour unions 28902-5-96
Income Tax Exemptions down there buy shares so that the base of the corporate ownership of their resources is far broader than it is here in Canada where the average working man and woman has not been able to purchase an equity in our Canadian economy because of our tax structure.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I raise a point of order. I think we are not discussing the budget now, but a motion; and I think the hon. member is not on the track.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXEMPTING REVENUES FROM CONTRIBUTIONS TO PENSION FUND
speechtext:
With respect, Mr. Speaker, my contention is to this effect: We have here a resolution which, if anything is done as a result of it, infers a greater proportion of our national savings being funnelled into the pension plan method of saving. We know, Mr. Speaker, that the pension plan method of saving does not result in investment in risk ventures. These savings do not go into the development of natural resources in our country or new industries. By definition, they cannot go into these avenues. The funds that go into the pension plans go into the trust type of saving method, possibly mortgages or office buildings, but nothing riskier than that.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, this is one of the great needs of our economy. We are faced with high corporate taxation and high taxation on property. Yes, we need to look after our old people, but we must also remember that we need to encourage far greater numbers of our people to invest in the equities in this country, to invest in new businesses, to invest in our natural resources so that our natural resources will not be controlled outside of this country. The more we put into pension plans, the less there will be in the total savings of this country to put into the risk area, the new development area, which we need to do so urgently.
For all these reasons I submit, with respect, Mr. Speaker, that my argument on this point is pertinent. There should be an over-all plan whereby a person who has been a citizen of this country, played his part in peace and war, brought up his family and contributed to the future of this country, paid taxes in this country for all his working life, will be looked after in dignity. Certainly, he should be looked after in such a fashion that he will not be in want during his senior years.
Along with that, I think we must consider the over-all picture. It is very easy for us to sit here in the back rows on both sides of this house and criticize government measures. It is because the entire picture must be considered that the preparation of a budget is most difficult. In considering this particular motion, Mr. Speaker, I must say that in my opinion the principle enunciated is a good one, mainly, that our older citizens should be

Income Tax Exemptions allowed $3000 a year without the state sticking its ever-grasping hand in their pockets. This is the very least that they should be allowed. However, I suggest that this should not be limited to pension plan type of savings which, by their definition, precludes their investment in the development of new industry or national resources where the need for risk capital is so urgent.
I think one of the greatest challenges in this country today, if we are going to live by the free enterprise system in which most of us believe, but which today has become a sort of laissez-faire free enterprise with small "s" socialism-welfarism if you like-is that our people's needs must be met to as great a degree as possible without complete over-all state planning, leaving a maximum of freedom to the individual so that he can provide for himself.
If we are going to have this type of free enterprise, and if free enterprise is to survive some of the great challenges facing it, we must strive for a more broadly based free enterprise system than we have now. We must do to a far greater degree what they have done with some success in the United States. We must encourage the average citizen to become a part owner of our industrial, corporate and natural resources, in order that the free enterprise system will mean something to him, and not remain the exclusive domain of those few who now own shares and those few who are so often quarrelled with by hon. members across the aisle. Our future should be held corporately by as many people as possible across the land, and I do not think this resolution tends towards that end, although its motive and intent are good.
I suggest that this resolution should be considered along with the other resolution brought forth by the government, and in the over-all if we consider the Canadian pensions act I think it will give a better way of life to our senior citizens, and will assure that those who have contributed so much to this country will in their declining years have some security and sufficient income to live in dignity. At the same time it will take into account the over-all needs of the country, and in particular the need for a greater proportion of the total savings of our people to go into equities, new industries and our natural resources, so that all our savings will not be held by trust companies and banks, but that more of our savings will go into the development of Canada.
If that is done, then tomorrow we will not see the situation that exists today where so many of our resources are held by people who do not owe any allegiance to Canada, and our natural resources will be controlled by Canadians through Canadian savings.

speechtext:

The minister called it a face the facts budget. I call it a hit and miss budget. He spent a great deal of time hitting at the previous government and all the time he missed the true significance of what a budget means or should do. In the ten years in which I have sat in this house I have never missed a budget speech.
