The gimmicks in this presentation demonstrate just how far hon. gentlemen opposite would like to go in developing an ever more complex bureaucracy. Just one such gimmick is the suggestion of a wage sharing contribution up to a maximum of $75 a month to any business giving employment to an unemployed person over the age of 45. The minister says the suggestion is not without difficulties and risks and will require careful administration and safeguards. While appreciating the intent, I say this scheme is so full of pitfalls it will need an army to administer.
I do not think I have time to deal at any length with the proposed 30 per cent tax on sale of shares of public companies listed on certain stock exchanges to non-residents, and since withdrawn. This has been gone into in detail by my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings as well as by others in this house. I would say, however, that before such a far reaching suggestion was proposed in this house the government should have had some knowledge as to the possibility of its administration. This afternoon the minister came to the conclusion that the proposal was not practicable for this budget. Why in the world did he not know this before causing such havoc on the financial markets? If these special advisers he has been admiring this afternoon were half as good as indicated, they should have known that the scheme was unworkable. What concerns me more is the minister's intimation on Friday, and again today, that if he could not overcome the administrative difficulties inherent in this tax, and could not re-introduce this particular iniquitous takeover penalty-and we now know he cannot-he proposes to introduce some new, some unknown curb on takeovers 
which will, perhaps, be just as destructive. Again today he said that something must be done. Does the minister propose to employ the same three brain trusters to conjure up this new and threatened impost, or will he rely on the tried, trusted and proven personnel of the finance department.
This afternoon the minister tried to justify his announcement of the withdrawal of the 30 per cent takeover tax at the opening of the house of Wednesday last. Why did he do that when never before have such announcements been made until after the closing of the financial markets? Was he frightened that due to the state of the market the country was going bankrupt? Why did he break all precedent? Any of his department advisers could have told him that this just was not done. The minister has gone into some detail to show us how he is trying to achieve 25 per cent Canadian participation in foreign-owned corporations. I agree with his objective.
I feel the one basic weakness in Canada's economy today is the huge annual payment of interest and dividends we must make to owners outside this country. When the previous government came into office we faced a trade deficit of some $753 million annually. We overcame that obstacle. We changed that deficit into a trade surplus over the last few years. In the meantime the balance of payments has been adversely affected by an ever increasing outgo of interest and dividends. I repeat that I agree with the minister's objectives, but is it the right method? Is it any more administratively possible than the ill-begotten $50,000 daily maximum permissible sales of Canadian corporations to non-residents? I do not think so. How is anyone to know from day to day the exact number of shares foreign-owned or Canadian-owned? For one thing stock transfer ledgers cannot be kept right up to the minute. What would happen if Canadian holdings were 24 per cent one day and 26 per cent the next? I have heard that the legal fraternity are already figuring out ways to try and beat the new proposals, such as allowing more than 25 per cent Canadian ownership of a participating common stock but non-voting, and have a small issue of voting stock. This might well help the imbalance of payments, but not the actual control in any way. Surely all this cannot help but create uncertainty and cause an outflow of foreign capital and even Canadian capital.
It seems to me that a more positive approach should be taken. Instead of penalizing the foreign investor, make it more attractive to the Canadian investor to invest in Canadian equities. Otherwise the foreign investor is definitely going to lose confidence in our economy, if he has not already done so. How

can he help it? I would like to give an actual illustration of just what this type of thing means. I will call the American subsidiary operating in Canada, to which I refer, company A. Company A has Canadian management. All its employees are Canadian. It has grown in 10 years from giving employment to 50 people to a position where it gives employment to 250. It has built up an export business. It has never paid a dividend to its American parent company. Some of its directors are Canadian. This company A had two deals pending whereby it would take over existing companies and in both cases could use its existing outlets to increase sales, increase exports, which are so important, and thereby increase employment which we all agree is paramount. If this proposal goes through I am afraid it will be the death knell of that increased employment. And to think this suggestion came from a government which had the temerity to say they could regain foreign confidence. I am as sure as can be that the foreign investor is today saying: "Oh for the good old days of the Conservative government when Canada followed sound financial policies".
There is a proposal in the budget to allow new manufacturing and processing enterprises, located in designated areas of slower growth, freedom from income tax for three years from their inception. Exactly what does this mean? Does inception mean incorporation or commencement of operations? We all know that the period between incorporation and the commencement of business often stretches into many months or more. Experience shows not too many enterprises make profits the first two or three years. Is extra depreciation as suggested of any real value during those years? New businesses if they are to qualify must be certified to have come into existence within 24 months following these measures becoming law. These terms are for a limited period. Are these enterprises going to find it advantageous to carry on after this period has expired? Personally, I feel section 40A of the Income Tax Act should be retained, as it is a continuing incentive to increased sales and, as a consequence, increased employment. It has not had a reasonable trial. I must agree with the objective desired, but I have grave doubts as to the actual application of these suggestions bringing about this objective. Only time will tell.
Then there is the proposed 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and production machinery and equipment. It will produce revenue, yes. But surely the minister is aware by now what a price he is going to pay by way of loss of jobs. I have heard it said that by the time sales tax is added to
The Budget-Mr. Monteith new machinery and also to the finished product, the actual building materials could be some 18 per cent higher in cost. The minister said in his budget speech that-
-there are good reasons for using the manufacturers sales tax rather than increased income taxes.
I wonder whether that is so, Mr. Speaker. As it is, he has chosen to stifle the construction business which is so vital to our over-all economy.
There have undoubtedly been thousands of protests about this move, but let me read a letter I received this morning. This letter, Mr. Speaker, is from the rector of the United Missionary Church in Listowel, Ontario, which is in my constituency. He says:
I am writing you regarding this 11 per cent federal tax which the Liberal government brought in in their recent budget. We are building a new church in the town of Listowel and were within four days of having our contract let and signed when the tax was imposed upon us. We feel this very keenly and it is going to work great hardship on our small congregation.
I noticed an article last evening in the Kitchener. Waterloo Record which I shall include in my letter. If there was the possibility of doing something or lifting the tax on senior citizens homes, would churches not also come under this category as they are a non-profit organization?
How this is going to help the economy of the country I cannot see, when the Liberal government said they were going to allow anyone who built a home in the winter a $500 premium and then a few days later a 11 per cent tax is put upon us. If there is anything you can do in this connection we would appreciate it greatly.
I would bring very forcibly to the attention of the minister the plight of these people.
This afternoon the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland) tried to give some explanation of the regulation and as to how the operation of this new tax was going to be handled. He mentioned that certain things were going to be exempt-hospitals, public institutions, municipalities and so on. Did he mean churches? I do not think so; there was no mention of them. This was the situation when, as I mentioned, they were within four days of signing a contract. The whole gist of the explanation of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland) this afternoon was ill founded in that this had not been decided upon before the budget was presented to the house. I would like to know, Mr. Speaker, whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) has any estimate as to the adjusted income which it is proposed he will receive because of the explanation of the Minister of National Revenue this afternoon, which course had not been determined at the time of the presentation of the budget. I think the whole thing is completely unsatisfactory and I believe, as the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) expressed it this

The Budget-Mr. Monteith afternoon, the removal of the exemption from sales tax of building supplies should not be proceeded with.
There are several other proposals in the budget, some of which I agree with at least in part. The minister has said the Glassco commission recommendations that may be expected to result in greater efficiency in the public service or in useful reductions in expenditure will be implemented as quickly as possible. I hope so. An economic council is to be set up. We proposed this last session and it was blocked by the opposition of the day.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not true.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is true. The minister says this government intends to maintain the fixed exchange rate at its present level. I believe it should. I cannot help but remind hon. members of the cry which went up from the present Minister of Finance and his colleagues at the time the present exchange rate was set by the previous government. They predicted gloom and doom, greatly increased prices and disaster to Canada. Now they agree with it. I feel we will all agree that excess expense accounts and high priced imported automobiles are unnecessary. It is proposed that section 18 of the Income Tax Act be repealed. This deals with lease option agreements. Due to abuses which have built up, I cannot disagree. I believe that the suggestion to make rebuilt or remanufactured goods subject to sales tax is going to hurt many small businesses. This proposal must be examined in detail at the resolution stage. I agree that the excise duty on exports of electrical energy should disappear. My colleague the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) has dealt more than adequately with the proposal that the Minister of National Revenue be vested with discretionary powers. I agree with him completely, particularly in light of the debate in this house some two years ago having to do with legislation concerning class or kind of goods made in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased, if I understood him correctly, that the minister this afternoon said he would have another look at this whole question.
There is a proposed amendment to stop a so-called device whereby a company that has experienced losses is purchased for the purpose of applying those losses against income from another business. I can understand the desire behind this amendment, but I would caution the government that there could be other objectives in purchasing such a company. Possibly by application of more knowledge, experience, sales outlets, and so on, such a company could honestly be expected to turn its losses into profits. This proposed amendment should be examined

closely. There are, of course, several customs tariff changes which must be studied in detail when we get into committee on the resolutions.
The minister has estimated a deficit of $565 million for the current fiscal year. To alleviate his position in subsequent years the minister has accelerated corporation income tax payments by two months. True enough, this will provide some additional nonrecurring revenue. He says it is desirable that corporations should pay their income tax as their income is earned to a greater extent than they do at present. Mr. Speaker, the minister left the impression that corporations would now be paying their income tax in a similar manner to that of individuals because they would both have to file their returns four months after their fiscal year end. I would point out that the individual is presumed to have approximately 100 per cent of his tax paid by the year end, either by way of deduction by his employer or by quarterly instalments. The corporation is not obliged to have its last instalment paid until four months after its year end. My only thought in mentioning this is that presumably some other finance minister might at some time in the future decide that he in turn would like to have available some nonrecurring revenue and there is still scope in this instance to move up payments another two months or even another four months.
I cannot help but predict an actual deficit of much larger proportions before the fiscal year is ended.
There will be large supplementary estimates before next March 31. The expected return from the sales tax on building supplies, machinery and equipment will not materialize, in my opinion, simply because construction will lag due to the increased costs, and consequently the industry will suffer. I would stress that this is not my main worry concerning the sales tax, but rather the resultant loss of jobs.
As to the position in 1964-65 one can only hazard a guess at this time. The suggested old age security increase for a full year would probably be in the neighbourhood of $130 million to $140 million. Increases in salaries paid by the government are, I believe, estimated to run some $65 million in a full year. To the best of my understanding a commitment has to all intents and purposes been made to the province of Quebec to increase its annual share of tax revenue. Naturally this would include all provinces. Any such step would obviously involve many, many millions of dollars. If this government fulfils all its promises, Mr. Speaker, I do

not see how it can escape a deficit approaching $1 billion in each of the next two years, unless it raises taxes.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must say that this budget has been born out of political expediency due to rash promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and his colleagues during the election campaign. But this is the accounting of the country's finances not only to Canadians but to the world. It is inexcusable that such a hash should be presented in this House of Commons. It is obvious that it was prepared without due consideration of all the possible implications. There is a lot of froth undoubtedly whipped up by the three wise men, but there is no substance, as would probably have been the case if the proper channels had been followed.
I utter harsh words, Mr. Speaker, but I feel they must be said. This afternoon the minister in some respects met certain complaints raised in this house during the past week. There is still much unexplained and his words cannot repair a great deal of damage already inflicted. His statement has done nothing to remove the calamitous uncertainty overhanging the securities market. Fortunes, I believe, have been made and lost these past few days. By the way, the Prime Minister this afternoon refused the request of the Leader of the Opposition for an inquiry into stock market transactions. What now can be done to bring this situation to an even keel? Certainly not the statement of the minister this afternoon.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having read the report of the Gordon commission on the economic prospects of Canada, following a survey which took place from 1955 to 1957, I was, in a way, pleased to find in the budget some concepts which were based on suggestions made in that report, more particularly those which tend to ensure the safeguarding of our industry and the gradual recovery of all we lost or never had.
Like all right-thinking and sincere Canadians, I would have liked a little more firmness, but I find that the government has, at most, confirmed the policy initiated by its political predecessor, which had been qualified as anti-American by some Liberals.
Mr. Speaker, to want Canadian ownership in Canada in no way indicates that we are nurturing feelings of animosity against anyone investing in this country. Be it far from
The Budget-Mr. M. Lessard me to think so, and I cannot understand how anyone can accuse of being anti-American those who want to show a proud spirit of national independance.
We in Quebec are accused of being troublesome fellows as regards confederation, because of our nationalist mind. I want to assure our English speaking fellow citizens that we are not "anti-everything". We are not "antiAmerican". No, we are pro-Canadian, that is all. We are not anti-English Canadian. No, we are pro-French Canadian and, as far as I am concerned, there is quite a difference. We are proud of our Canada, we are proud of the dual culture prevailing in this country. We are fighting for biculturalism, because we want Canada to be different from the United States.
We appeal to your co-operation, we want you to understand the issue and realize the urgency of acting in this matter before it is too late. Let us become aware of the superiority our Canadian nation will get from biculturalism.
I would like to quote here the remarks which a prominent member of the London privy council made in the course of a lecture he was giving in Montreal a few years ago. He had asked the audience:
What is a French Canadian?
Whereupon a young newspaperman told him from the front row:
Sir, a French Canadian is a man who has acquired the two greatest cultures in the world. The French-Latin culture which is made of sensibility and subtlety, and the Anglo-Saxon culture which is made of honesty and on immense practical sense.
And the lecturer replied:
Sir, this is the best explanation possible for the marvelous behaviour, the peerless value I always noticed when your solicitors came before the privy council in London.
Mr. Speaker, this in my opinion is an unequivocal proof of the value of our two cultures. This is why we must together extend that heritage to the greatest possible number of our fellow citizens and to those who will come after us.
I would not for a moment entertain the idea of compelling all Canadians to become bilingual and to acquire perfect mastery of the wide scope of our two cultures; this would certainly be marvellous, but it would not in any way be justified practically.
Yet, I believe that it is logical to expect in the near future that 10 per cent of our population will be more or less gained to the

The Budget-Mr. M. Lessard principle of biculturalism and will be able to occupy administrative positions in the public service and in all the areas of our social and economic structures.
Thus constituted, the Canadian nation would obtain an increasing recognition and a great many of our fellow Canadians would occupy prominent positions in the international field.
At present, we are experiencing growing pains, we are a new nation which grew fast and has some difficulties finding a suit which will fit its continued development.
We are in search of our true features, those our fathers of 1867 wanted us to have. I feel sure that with a little good will here and there we shall build a strong Canada respected by all.
Canada needs leaders able to set on a very high plane the ideal to be reached and to indicate clearly the paths leading to it.
I note with satisfaction that for some time we have been making progress towards greater mutual understanding and I dare hope that such is only the beginning and that we shall remain in those good dispositions.
Mr. Speaker, we are now examining the budget presented to us by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), and I should like to refer to the tone strongly flavoured with political bias in which the speech was read last Thursday. Personally, I deeply regret it because I thought very highly of the minister who always seemed without pretence, humble and sincere; what I particularly liked about him was the fact that he did not have that detestable political arrogance, so detrimental to the high regard in which politics should be held.
What comforts me, however, is the fact that I suspect him not to be the author of those uncalled for remarks but I think that they come rather from one of his colleagues whose heart is still filled with the resentment collected during the last six years spent in the gloom of the opposition.
The minister did not have to attack a defeated opponent to justify some of his omissions in the budget or to make Canadians gulp down the increase of some $100 million in taxes which the small wage earner will have to pay.
In this, he carries on the policy of his predecessors who always made the little fellow pay for the administration's errors, while helping the big man accumulate millions, because, as far as they are concerned, there can be no question of tightening one's belt. Indeed we have always seen them this way.
I hope that the minister will not let himself be guided by such bad advisers, and that
[Mr. Lessard (Lake St. John).!

he will, as he did before, serve us his own ideas, which all hon. members have appreciated during the short period of time the hon. member for Davenport has been sitting in this house.
I can assure the minister that he still has my esteem though I am aware of the bad influence to which he is exposed from those who surround him.
I would like to point out to the minister that Canadian products find it very difficult to compete on external markets and this will become more and more so.
May I quote an excerpt from an item published in the Financial Post of February last, in which an economist who investigated the situation in Germany-a situation always held up as an international example of planned revival-and which reads as follows:
(Text):
Its industries no longer have the enormous backlogs of unfilled orders that characterized the past decade and its exporters are doing business in world markets where oversupply and overcapacity increasingly are the rule.
(Translation):
If I refer to his statement, I find that he points out that, at the present time, Germany must, to maintain its level of economic growth, go more and more on the export market, on that market that is already completely saturated by various products. Therefore, I wonder what we, in Canada, are able to do, what we can contemplate to compete with such countries as Germany, France, Belgium and England.
In secondary industry, I am of the opinion that we will meet strong competition and our chances of success are slim. I do not want to be pessimistic but I think that Canada, like the United States, should look within her own borders. That is what President Kennedy did in the United States, our southern neighbours.
In my opinion, that is what we should also do north of the 45th parallel if we really want to find a practical solution to our unemployment problem. I wonder whether the Minister of Finance realizes that he cannot achieve this by himself, that without the co-operation of his cabinet colleagues, the possibility of success is slight. Nevertheless, there are solutions within reach, but he persists in disregarding them.
Everyone admits that the number of our secondary industries must be increased.
Everyone admits that we must produce ourselves everything that is physically and economically possible to produce.

If the minister looks around, he will see that in the government administration and in the crown corporations, hundreds of millions of dollars, resulting from taxes paid by the citizens, are used each year for the purchase of materials, machines and services directly from foreign countries. Now, those things could be produced here in a large proportion. I am convinced-as he is himself- that that is the only way to stem unemployment at present. It would be interesting for the people to see what influences, let alone bribes, are at work, before those purchases from abroad are made.
It is enough to mention here the strange bargaining that is now taking place in the eventual purchase of jet airplanes for the Trans-Canada Air Lines. According to all evidences, the Caravelle seems to be the best choice. Its efficiency has been tested from all viewpoints and we now have a choice between three airplanes which are actually Caravelles, or modified versions of that aircraft. We have been offered the Caravelles and we were told that they may be built in Canada.
The Minister of Finance might seize this opportunity to restore our external trade balance, and, in so doing, he would get out of the tight corner where he has been put by our international deficits. Those $250 million which Trans-Canada Air Lines is going to spend could be spent in Montreal on that order which, placed with Canadair, would give work to several thousand Canadian technicians and qualified workers.
We have seen in the press where another Canadian company-not a crown corporation this time-is thinking of building 18 cargo-boats at a cost of more than $1 billion. And where would these ships be built? In Japan.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I feel that if a billion dollar contract were granted to shipbuilding companies in Canada, in the province of Quebec or in the maritime provinces, the Minister of Finance would surely find it easier to balance his budget or, at least, to restore our foreign trade balance. I told him the other day that he might possibly bring pressure to bear. He answered that he was not allowed to make any pressure but I feel that he should at least make suggestions which would be more appropriate at this time of the year when we are faced with yet another deficit of half a billion dollars for the year 1963-64.
Last Monday, we opened a debate on certain alleged indiscretions or certain methods which are reported to have been followed for the preparation of the budget. The members of our group did not want to have a full debate on that point because we 28902-5-97
The Budget-Mr. M. Lessard knew that it would lead us nowhere in the long run since, at ten o'clock in the evening, there would be nothing left to say and we would have gained nothing for our trouble.
However, that does not mean that we approve the manner in which the budget was prepared. We feel it is most improper to call in strangers for the establishment of the policy under which our country is to be governed during the coming year because that could enable some people and their associates to make undue profits overnight at the expense of a defenceless and powerless public.
Nevertheless, I doubt that the minister set a precedent in doing so. It is most likely that something similar was done in the past and if the hon. gentlemen who sit on this side of the house and who accuse the minister of unspeakable actions, took the trouble of reviewing their administration in years gone by, they might And that they acted in a somewhat similar fashion if not exactly the same way. Having heard considerable talk about this matter these past few days, I feel this issue has been sufficiently thrashed out and should be dropped.
Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance introduces another budget next year-I am doubtful because of certain rumours going round-I suggest that he should invite every representative public body to submit briefs on fiscal matters. Subsequently, he could look into those briefs in consultation with the senior officers of his department and, in the light of the suggestions submitted to him, he would then be in a position to prepare a budget in the best interests of the country.
Everyone admits that the Minister of Finance cannot know everything and it is normal that he should seek the required information among the general public or probe public opinion. Therefore, he should call upon representative bodies to submit briefs every year in the fiscal and economic fields, which he could study afterwards in conjunction with his officers and experts. On the other hand, I hope he will not always go to Toronto to seek experts. He should look elsewhere, in Montreal or in Vancouver. Anyhow, I hope that with the assistance of his experts and senior officials, he will be able to draft a budget that will be acceptable to everybody. To summarize, I wish him greater success than the last time.
In his 1957 report on Canada's economic prospects the hon. minister stated that full employment contributes to inflation but, quite recently, in answer to one of my questions on that statement, he told me that I would find the answer in the efforts made by the government in its budget to eliminate unemployment.

The Budget-Mr. M. Lessard
Unfortunately, I have to advise the minister that many points of his budget are entirely negative and that they checkmate every effort made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen) to reduce unemployment.
The minister did suggest a few measures to bring about economic recovery but with only one of his negative actions, he has wrecked the positive accomplishments which one could expect from the budget.
The harmful and backward measure I am referring to is the 11 per cent tax imposed upon building materials. The minister knows better than anybody else, since he received all those telegrams and messages, that this tax is unpopular. Of course, the question is not whether the tax is popular or not, for we all know that there is no such thing as a popular tax, and we are not concerned presently with the popularity of the tax itself but with its devastating effects.
Both the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance have stated that unemployment should be eliminated, that it has lasted too long already; of course, no one can disagree with that. But when on the one hand he makes minor concessions and on the other introduces taxes to kill the advantages offered through other measures, we wonder what the members of the cabinet plan to do with such a procedure.
Mr. Speaker, this new tax shows the state of confusion which pervades the cabinet. They take back with one hand more than they gave with the other and each department seems to work in isolation.
Following the coming to power of a Liberal government a few members of which are prominent planners and economists, after all the promises they had made, we believed that we would see the unemployment problem solved and everything going perfectly smooth. But how disappointed are the Canadians. One is wondering whether one of these days one will not be asked to establish a department of planning to plan some of the government's planners. Things have reached that point.
The Minister of Labour offered a $500 bonus to those who will build during the winter months. The Minister of Finance imposed an 11 per cent tax on building materials. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland) proposed to reduce by one quarter of 1 per cent the interest on mortgage loans, but where would all that lead us? If the left hand doesn't know what the right hand is doing, we would be better off if nobody gave anything, since in the end the cost to

government for collecting taxes and giving back bonuses or some other kind of grants will consequently reduce the government tax revenues. In a way, we are carrying water with a bottomless pail and I wish to stress that the people are not getting anything out of it.
The people were expecting much, they have been utterly disappointed, those thousands of Canadians who are hungry and lack the necessities of life. Following the promises made by this government in the last two general elections, we were entitled to expect a much more positive and speedy action from the Liberals. Some will say that election promises are just as good as a drinker's determination. And once more, unfortunately, this proverb has been confirmed, yet there will be some to wonder why some voters are cynical and do not have any respect for those who administer the business of this country. Keep on like that, keep on protecting capitalism, and a day will come, which is not too far away where we will fall into the quagmire where other countries have foundered into most complete anarchy.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether the government are aware of the situation, but I feel it is time they react because pretty soon it will be too late.
In order to encourage the establishment of industries in depressed areas, the minister provides certain allowances and, by the way, I should like to know on what basis the Minister of Finance and the members of cabinet will determine in what depressed areas industries will be allowed to settle in order to enjoy the benefits provided for in the budget. That would be a good thing to know so that it does not work to the advantage of the richer areas.
Besides, the solution provided by the multiplication of secondary industries cannot be carried out overnight and something more will have to be done to eliminate unemployment quickly.
Mr. Speaker, I had expected much more from the municipal development bank and I must say that I am greatly deceived. I realize that many amendments will be needed to Bill C-76 before we can expect from it substantial benefits to alleviate unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that time flies. I shall summarize by saying that this budget as a whole is disappointing. It contained some interesting proposals, but the withdrawal of the 30 per cent tax-not so much the 30 per cent tax in itself, but the principle which it confirmed-has somewhat disappointed me.

I think that the Liberal party went right off the track. But considering the fact that the government has now been in office for only two months and that they had many promises to fulfil, we shall grant them a reprieve so that they may either redeem themselves or to prove completely before the people that they are incompetent.
I am sure the people will accept for another period of time to tolerate the government they have elected. Now the opportunity is being given to them to judge the two old line parties. As a matter of fact, they have already dealt with the Conservatives and they are now trying the Liberals who went into retreat for a few years. The people, probably convinced that the Liberals had been chastened by their penance, realize now, a few months later, that the government is changed, but that we have actually been keeping the same administrators and that we should not expect great solutions to the problems facing the nation and the Canadian economy.
The government has submitted its budget and the minister has assumed full responsibility for it as he has assumed the responsibility for the withdrawal of the 30 per cent tax. We criticized him. We submitted proposals to him, as it is our duty to do, and we are asking him to take them under consideration. Time will tell who provided the right answer to the problems facing our country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with the amendment which has been proposed by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). I should like to deal with it in two parts, first the part which deals with the procedures in the preparation of the budget, and I shall read the words contained in that part of the amendment:
This house regrets that the Minister of Finance by failing to maintain the constitutional practice of the essential secrecy of the budget has seriously weakened public confidence;
I shall deal with that point first; and then I shall go on to deal with the balance of the amendment which has reference to the contents of the budget itself.
I am one of those who is new in the house, but with some experience in government as a civil servant, I can understand the anxiety of hon. members that the essential secrecy of the budget should be maintained.

97i
The Budget-Mr. Sharp At the same time I must say I deplore the insinuations which reflect on the honesty and integrity of certain persons who have been named in this house without any evidence whatsoever to support those insinuations and reflections.
May I deal with the procedures? I naturally agree with the hon. member for Digby-An-napolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) that secrecy is absolutely essential. If there were any suggestions in anything that was said in this house that the secrecy of the budget had been in any way impaired I would be one of those who would vote for the amendment. But there have been no charges made of any kind, and when the Leader of the Opposition was challenged to make such charges he flunked. I know the reasons why it is of great importance, indeed, essential, that secrecy be maintained not only because of the importance of the question itself but also because we all recognize that no one should be in a position to exploit prior knowledge for personal gain. This is a principle upon which we all agree. I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to another financial operation conducted a few years ago in which there was great opportunity for personal gain for individuals having prior knowledge.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Make the charge.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am making no charges. I am dealing with this incident, and I hope the hon. member will listen very carefully to what was done by the opposition of that day. I am referring, of course, to the conversion loan. This was an operation of the previous government the financial implications of which were at least as large as, indeed far larger than those provided by this budget or by any budget presented to the house with respect to opportunities for profit by any investment dealer privileged to have inside information. What did the previous administration do at the time of the conversion loan? The loan was to be announced to the public on a Monday. On the previous Thursday, 14 investment dealers and bankers were assembled in Ottawa. On Friday, 28 more were assembled and these gentlemen were asked to advise on the technical details of how this mammoth financial operation should be handled. On the Saturday, about 200 of the senior members of investment and banker institutions were added to the circle of people being given inside information.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense; sheer nonsense.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All these people were sworn to secrecy. Many could have profited greatly by breaking that oath. But there has never

The Budget-Mr. Sharp been any suggestion that any improper use was made of their information. It was, and is, a great tribute to the integrity of Canadians and of those individuals who were privy to this inside information from which they could have profited, had they broken their oath-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? When he becomes minister of finance will he not consult bankers before he negotiates a loan?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is exactly the point that I think ought to be borne in mind by all hon. members. There are occasions when it is necessary to do these things. I am not criticizing the previous government for having done what it did. That is not the point of my speech.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister if he thinks matters pertaining to the budget can be assimilated to any other matters with regard to which the government might seek advice.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I suggest to the hon. member that the essence of the case is the same. There is no greater need for secrecy about the budget than there is about a loan from which millions of people could have made a profit.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think I have been charitable in allowing interruptions, and I should like to finish what I have to say. I believe there is one more speaker, at least, and I should like him to have an opportunity of addressing the house.
When my colleagues were in opposition- I was not here at that time; I was earning a living-they criticized and rightly criticized the conversion loan with respect to its financial effects. They never suggested the government had been wrong to rely on the honesty of Canadians. They never suggested that information which the government gave to people in a position to profit by it was in fact used for such a purpose. That is the distinction. The present Leader of the Opposition, at that time prime minister presumably knew how the conversion loan was handled. Presumably he knew that many men who derived their income from financial operations were given information from which they could have profited had they broken their oath of secrecy and used that knowledge for their own ends or for the companies who paid their salaries.
The Leader of the Opposition was prime minister when 200 people were trusted in this way, yet he now pretends to see a con-

flict of interests when two people are trusted. By insinuation and innuendo, but never by charges, he suggests there was impropriety. What can one say of this? I can say only that the whole issue upon which so much of the time of the house has been spent in the last few days is a false issue. Canadians who take oaths, at least in my experience, can be trusted. The right hon. gentleman's government, when he was in power, acted on that assumption.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where is the evidence?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, you trusted them. The right hon. gentleman's government trusted them in their hundreds. My colleague, the Minister of Finance, has trusted two.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He said three.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Four.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Five.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Any more?
The Leader of the Opposition was right.
I am not criticizing him. He was right when he gave his trust. I am not suggesting there was anything wrong about it. But I do suggest he is wrong when he insinuates there was a betrayal of trust, a betrayal of budget secrets, because two men were brought from the financial community to assist the present Minister of Finance.
As all hon. members are aware and, more particularly, those who recently occupied the treasury benches, the budget, as well as other form of legislative action, is becoming more complicated as governments necessarily intervene in trying to influence the economy. It is necessary to bring in outside experts of one sort or another to help governments as temporary officials in departments or as members of commissions. In my opinion this is a useful development. I have served in government and I have served outside. I think some exchange of government specialists with businessmen from time to time on special assignments is a most useful development, and I hope it continues. I do not look on it as any reflection on the civil service that these two, four, or as many as you like to say, came in to help the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) in preparing the budget and other legislation which was part of the economic program. I should like to pay tribute to the men, many of whom I have known when I was a permanent civil servant myself, many hundreds, indeed perhaps thousands, who from time to time gave their services to the government without hope of gain, many with great cuts in their incomes, just in order to make a contribution to the public welfare.
Although perhaps this is redundant, I should like for a moment to repeat in a

different form two or three of the points made today by my colleague the Minister of Finance when he was dealing with the three consultants who have been under discussion in this house. As hon. members know, no budget has been debated in this house for two years. There was a budget last April but it was never debated. In fact, there has been no accounting of the financial affairs of this country for two years. No opportunity has been given hon. members of this house to discuss the financial affairs of the country thoroughly and at length until now. Somebody suggested to me the other day that in view of the criticism which has been made of this budget it is small wonder that the previous government did not bring one down for a couple of years. It was also most important, not only for a financial accounting of this country, which was so long overdue, but because of the economic problems being faced by this country, that a budget should be brought down as quickly as possible, and for that reason the Minister of Finance had to resort to special procedures in order to get help in the preparation of his budget.
We could have proceeded otherwise. We could have delayed this budget for quite some time. But I suggest to hon. members that it is important to have a budget even if the opposition does not thing so, as their actions show. Moreover, I think the Minister of Finance was right when in his budget he brought forward part of the program of this government for employment and the supply of those incentives which are so needed if this country is to make the progress that it should be making. It was also necessary to bring it in at once if these measures were to have the desired effect with regard to next year's unemployment. This meant a heavy work load on the Department of Finance, where there is already a shortage of senior staff. It would have been impossible, as those on the opposition benches who were formerly in government knew, to have been able to get permanent civil servants at this time to do this work.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) suggested that these gentlemen wrote the budget. I am sure the hon. gentleman knows that, in the final analysis, no one writes the budget except the minister, and he gets help from many officials. These officials who are under criticism here had no executive power. They had no power to make any decisions. They were merely advisory. They were in the same position as were any permanent civil servants.
Let us look at the position as it emerged. Those on the treasury benches recognize as much as everyone else the special necessity
The Budget-Mr. Sharp for secrecy in connection with the preparation of the budget. This is a tradition which is well established and certainly one which my colleague the Minister of Finance honours, and I am sure will honour regardless of how many budgets he brings in. Everyone who worked on this budget was sworn to secrecy. There has never been any suggestion that they were not. Under the circumstances it is obviously better that anybody working on the budget or any other financial legislation be paid by the government. This government would not lightly depart from that general rule. I was interested in the observation of my colleague the Minister of Finance when he said today that perhaps in a technical sense he had departed from a convention. But there was no suggestion by anyone that these individuals were in any way prejudiced or hampered in the discharge of the temporary duties they had undertaken by the fact that they had not been taken off the payroll of the companies concerned, but paid by them during the temporary period they were employed in the government; nor has anyone suggested that this made any essential difference to the conflict of interests.
May I go back to a much more important occasion when there were at least 200 people brought in and given inside information. Nobody suggested at that time that they should be taken off their payrolls while they gave temporary advice to the government on a matter on which they might have made a fortune had they broken their oaths of secrecy. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that if these men who are from time to time called in to give temporary service to the government are required to sever all their connections with the companies they serve, it will be very difficult indeed for this government to get help from time to time, or for that matter for the next government, to whichever party it may belong, to get the help it requires if individuals have to terminate their careers in private business for a short period, and then return to them. I think this is an impracticable state of affairs in the world in which we live today where, as I say, it is from time to time necessary for the government to get technical help of one kind or another.
If there were any risk whatsoever that budget secrecy would be destroyed by asking people to come and serve the government for a temporary period, then everyone would agree that it would be better to do without them even if their services would be invaluable. But it never occurred to anybody concerned, least of all, I am sure, to my colleague the Minister of Finance, that there was any risk. The probity of these gentlemen is beyond question. It has not been challenged by the

The Budget-Mr. Sharp Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) nor by any other hon. member of this house. These men, as I have said, were not brought in to make decisions; they were not brought in for executive responsibility of any kind; they were brought in to advise.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What horrible advice.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-twisted, or slanted, or influenced the proposals made by the Minister of Finance is simply making an allegation that is about as unconvincing as any I have ever heard. The record of the Minister of Finance, his personality, his experience, his reputation establish beyond doubt that he is a man who would not be influenced, and particularly would not be influenced in ways which, with his business experience, he would be more alert than anyone to protect if there were any question of special interest at work.
So we are left with one other possibility, that these men leaked budget secrets. This is one charge of substance that could be made in this matter, but it has not been made. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was challenged to make it today and, as I said before, he flunked.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe there is another hon. member who wishes to speak on this subject. I am sorry I have taken up so much time on this point. However, may I just conclude my remarks by again repeating the words-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How about repetition?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me again repeat the words of the first paragraph of the amendment:
This house regrets that the Minister of Finance by failing to maintain the constitutional practice of the essential secrecy of the budget has seriously weakened public confidence.
I say to the house that this is a very serious charge. I am surprised-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Set up the inquiry, then.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -that the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings should have put his amendment in these words-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In such a moderate way.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -and may I suggest that if there is any substance in this charge, the charges should be made now.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, the minister said a few moments ago that anyone making a charge should make it now. Now he says that I made a charge in this amendment. He said that if a charge was made, the government would set up a committee. According to his words I made a charge; then let the government set up a committee.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My concluding words, Mr. Speaker, are these, that all there is in the first paragraph of this amendment is innuendo and insinuation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a good deal of interest this afternoon to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). I must say that I have never listened to a weaker defence. The minister who came in here on June 13 and made one of the most belligerent and partisan budget speeches that I have ever listened to at least appeared today in a much humbler and wiser mood. I think the author of "Troubled Canada" will now be able to write an autobiography called, "A Troubled Canadian".
Mr. Speaker, this is a thoroughly bad budget presented with an unbelievable amount of fumbling, bungling and ineptitude. Let me

deal first of all with the matter of the presentation of the budget itself. The ineptitude is shown up on two counts. First of all there were the three budgeteers from Bay street. At first the minister tried to evade this question, and then some five hours later he came into the house and admitted that they had been brought in as consultants. These men cannot be compared, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) compared them, with some consultants brought in for consultation for one or two hours. These were men who were hired for several weeks and yet were retained on the payrolls of their respective companies. This arouses the whole question of the conflict of interest. It is not enough for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to stand up and say "Let somebody make a charge". It is not enough that the public interest be protected; it must manifestly be seen to be protected.
This afternoon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) beat his breast about the innuendoes and insinuations that have been hurled at these innocent victims of political chicanery, but he himself put them in that position by bringing them here and making them privy to the preparation of the budget while they continued to be employed by investment dealers. It is only natural that newspapers and others who have seen strange happenings on the stock exchange should draw conclusions which may not be warranted. But the minister himself has put them in this awkward and embarrassing position. I suggest that when the Prime Minister gets his report from the stock exchanges, as he has promised to do, it will warrant a thorough and complete investigation into the block trading that took place immediately prior to and immediately after the presentation of the budget.
The other ineptitude was shown in the handling of the 30 per cent takeover tax which the minister announced in the house on June 13; then on June 19, less than a week later, he came into the house and said he was withdrawing the tax because of administrative difficulties. Mr. Speaker, was he not aware of these administrative difficulties? Had he not consulted his officials prior to putting this tax into the budget? Had there been no consultation with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland) and his officials? What was there six days later that made administrative difficulties more apparent than had been six days before? This was the very essence of ineptitude. When the minister was asked on the 19th of this month, last Wednesday, he said no one had been informed about this except the Prime Minister and some members of the cabinet. But on Friday last we found that all three of the budgeteers from Bay
The Budget-Mr. Douglas street had been informed prior to this statement being made in the house. The minister may talk about being misunderstood but to me this was a matter of misleading the house. I suggest that no member can mislead the house without receiving the censure of the house. I want to say that the presentation of this budget is the acid test of the Prime Minister's sense of responsibility to parliament and to the conduct of public affairs in this country, and it will be for him to decide whether or not the minister in question should continue to occupy the portfolio he now holds.
The outrageous manner in which the budget was presented, Mr. Speaker, should not be allowed to obscure the fact that the budget itself is a dismal failure in the light of the economic problems that confront this country and the state of the Canadian economy. There are four things about the budget that I would criticize. First of all, it is not an expansionary-budget. It is a regressive and schizophrenic budget. It does nothing effectively to regain control of the Canadian economy and it does nothing about increasing Canada's export trade. I doubt that in the time at my disposal I can deal with all four points but I will deal with as many as I can.
First of all, I say this it not an expansionary budget. The crying need of this country is to remove unemployment by promoting a higher rate of economic growth. This will not be done by this budget. In the first place, it will not be done by allowing business corporations to keep a larger share of their profits as an incentive to investment. From 1957 to 1961 real investment declined by 11 per cent and in the same period of time business savings increased by 4 per cent.
Nor will we cure unemployment and promote economic growth by providing larger profits to business as an incentive to investment. During the period 1955 to 1957 inclusive the corporate tax burden was greater per dollar of profit than it has been since 1957. Yet this was the period of our greatest investment boom. Why? Not because profits were greater-they were less-but because there was anticipation of an increased effective demand. That effective demand did not materialize but the fact is that this was the incentive, and the need in our economy today is to increase effective demand so that a larger portion of our population in Canada can buy the goods and services that our economy is capable of producing in this technological age.
There are two ways in which we can increase this effective demand. The first is by injecting massive doses of social capital into our economy in order to put the unemployed to work and to increase productivity. We should use the Bank of Canada and we should

The Budget-Mr. Douglas be prepared to accept the need for extensive deficits and deficit financing. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) said this afternoon that he had only three alternatives. He said he had to increase income and corporation taxes or he had to increase the general sales tax or he had to impose a sales tax on building materials and production machinery. He said that these were the three alternatives if you accept the premise that we must move toward a balanced budget.
There we have the kernel of the whole matter. We in this group do not accept this premise. As a matter of fact, when I listened to the minister delivering his budget speech I thought he had found an old budget speech of Mr. Fleming's lying in the office and had simply dusted it off and brought it before the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Never.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Someone has said that the more things change the more they are the same. This country need not be afraid of deficit financing. As my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) pointed out, Sweden, which has full employment and a higher standard of income per capita than Canada, has a deficit of nearly 3 per cent of its gross national product, twice that of Canada. We in this country could double our deficit financing without being in serious difficulty. We would not lose by it. In the long run increased productivity, what we would save by putting the unemployed to work and increased economic activity would bring the government back a great many economic returns both in tax revenue and in other ways.
But the government has done just the opposite. Instead of seeking to stimulate the economy it has applied an 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and production machinery and this will have the effect inevitably of slowing down construction. This is going to have the effect of throwing people out of work. This is going to stop some of the building programs that were being planned. This is why I say this is a schizophrenic budget. We have set in motion two great forces going in opposite directions, the one cancelling out the other. On the other hand we say we have got a budget that is going to promote full employment and on the other hand we impose taxes that will produce unemployment and stop economic growth and development.
The municipal development and loan fund will help, of course, but social capital cannot be supplied only by the municipalities.

What about the provincial governments, and the federal government carrying their share of supplying social capital? There is nothing in this budget that will do that. The minister knows better. The minister began his speech by making a good Keynesian case for deficit financing and then, having made his proper genuflections to the Mecca of Keynesian economics, he took off across the arid sands of orthodox financing that lead to the land of unemployment and economic stagnation.
The other thing that needs to be done to increase effective demand is to put purchasing power into the pockets of that section of our economy which is unable to buy the goods and services which this country has to sell. We do this by putting unemployed people to work at decent wages. We do this by increasing the old age pension and lowering the age to 65 years. You do it by increasing family allowances and veterans pensions. You do it by lowering the income tax on the lower and middle income groups and you do it by lowering sales taxes, not increasing them, so as to lower the cost of living, thereby increasing the purchasing power of great sections of our population.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that there is nothing in this budget designed to promote full employment. There is nothing in this budget that will help promote economic growth. This budget is a regressive budget. At the present time federal taxes are divided roughly into 60 per cent direct taxes and 40 per cent indirect taxes. When the provinces and municipalities are included, the average Canadian pays about half his taxes indirectly and half his taxes directly. There is no more vicious or regressive tax than an indirect tax. The minister took the one place to find the money he thought he needed, not in the field of direct taxes, not by a capital gains tax, not by taxing those who have more than they need, but by placing an additional $700 on the cost of a small house. This means that a man purchasing that house under N.H.A. and paying 6i per cent over 25 years will have $1,377 added to the cost of purchasing that house. This is why we say this is a regressive tax, placing a burden upon those who are least able to bear it. It is for this reason, Mr. Speaker, we in this group cannot support this budget, nor will we be associated with the cloud of suspicion that has surrounded its presentation.
On the other hand, on March 27 last on a national television program, I made a commitment to the people of this country that if a minority government were elected in Canada we would give that minority government,

whichever party formed it, a reasonable period of time in which to carry out its program for economic recovery. This government has not yet had a reasonable period of time. They have not yet made much use of the time they have had. However, we believe they are entitled to a reasonable period of time. Therefore we find ourselves in a dilemma. We are not prepared to vote confidence in this budget or in the manner of its presentation. On the other hand, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) is not only a statement of opinion, with which opinion we largely agree, but written into that amendment is the provision that the government should be turned out and that a general election should be held.
We do not believe the people of this country want an election. This would be the third general election in 15 months. We believe that the people of this country want this parliament to get on with the job of governing Canada. For that reason, we of the New Democratic party, will abstain from voting on this amendment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame, shame.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: By abstaining from voting we are saying to the government that we are prepared to see you stay in office in the hope that you will do something to implement the promises you made to the people of Canada. But by abstaining, we are also stating that we have no confidence in this budget, that we will not be associated with this dismal budget and the disastrous consequences which we believe will flow from its implementation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order; it being nine forty-five o'clock, it is my duty, pursuant to section 5 of standing order 58, to interrupt these proceedings forthwith and put the question on any amendment now before the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
After the vote has been taken I wish to rise on a point of order before determination and tabulation takes place.
On a point of order, not because it will affect the result at all, but with a view to preventing a precedent being established here, I wish to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that no member in the house, in his seat in the house, can refrain from declaring his vote. That has been an accepted principle throughout the years. I refer to Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure at page 381 where it is stated:
If a member of the Commons who has heard the question put does not vote, and the attention of the Speaker is directed to the fact, the latter will call upon him to declare on which side he votes; and his name will be recorded accordingly.
The only exception is where there is a motion not properly before the house. I direct your attention to Hansard 1956, volume 5 at pages 4553 and 4554 when the Conservative party, at that time in opposition, did not vote on a course of action submitted by Mr. Speaker. During the taking of the vote, Mr. Speaker said:
Those who are opposed will please rise.
Hon. Mr. Drew said:
We are not voting because there is no question properly before the house.
When a question is properly before the house it is requisite that members shall vote if they are in the house. That goes back to May 12, 1879, and it has never been departed from since. At that time a certain hon. gentleman, a Mr. LaRue, voted although he had been paired. Sir John Macdonald said that it rested with the hon. member to say whether his vote should remain on the record or not. If he chose to have his name recorded it was for him to say so. Then these significant words:
Every member in the house, if called upon was compelled to vote, and, even if a gentleman got up and stated that he had paired the house could compel him to vote, because, if he had paired, he must leave the house before the vote was taken.
That was the general principle. I raise this point at this time not because it will in any way alter the result of this vote, but a precedent of this kind is detrimental to the proper processes of parliamentary procedure, if members sitting in the house in their places say that they will not vote on a measure before the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the first place I think it would be helpful if you would rule on the

right of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) to raise a point of order before the vote has been announced and during the taking of the vote. Apart from that matter, the point which the hon. gentleman now makes with such emphasis apparently did not occur to him when he was prime minister and leader of the house when, in a vote in the last session of parliament the hon. member for Halifax, one of the former prime minister's followers, abstained from voting and that abstention was not mentioned or noted by the right hon. gentleman.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry, it is after ten o'clock.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -the result of a vote must be announced before any hon. member can say he was paired. Therefore no question can be raised till the vote is announced and the pairs are also announced.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I might say immediately that when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Dief-enbaker) raises these interesting matters I am always impressed at first with the experience of the right hon. gentleman and his knowledge. However, he referred to Bourinot and the citation to which he referred involved an incident many years ago. Sir Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, sixteenth edition, page 434, refers to the British house of commons and says:
Practice in the House of Commons-A similar rule formerly obtained in the House of Commons, but in session 1906, in connection with the changes made in taking divisions which have been already mentioned, the house agreed to a new standing order-now S.O. No. 33-which provided that a member might vote in a division although he had
not heard the question put, and that a member was not obliged to vote although he was in the house when the question was put.
Then dealing with a very similar situation, Mr. Glen, as reported in the debates of the House of Commons for September 28, 1945, page 542, said:
Mr. Speaker, this question has always been somewhat confused in this House of Commons. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) spoke of an incident which occurred at a time when he was a member of the house. He has pointed out that on that occasion the matter was brought to the attention of the house and that the hon. member in question was requested to record his vote.
This is the important part.
A year ago when we were dealing with a revision of the rules this matter was considered carefully by hon. members of the committee. At that time they did not think they should make a recommendation to the house in this connection. The position I always took when I occupied the Speaker's chair was that an hon. member who was in the house should record his vote; but if he did not do so the Chair had no power to compel him to do so.
So in accordance with previous precedents I must regretfully reject the suggestion.
